articles.title: Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Kenya committed $160 million over ten years to protect 173,000 square kilometers (roughly 67,000 square miles, or 17.3 million hectares) across some of the least-disturbed land in Africa: the Great Rift Valley, the Maasai Mara, and surrounding biodiversity areas. The program is called Thamani Asili, which means “value of […]
The post Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Kenya committed $160 million over ten years to protect 173,000 square kilometers (roughly 67,000 square miles, or 17.3 million hectares) across some of the least-disturbed land in Africa: the Great Rift Valley, the Maasai Mara, and surrounding biodiversity areas.

The program is called Thamani Asili, which means “value of nature” in Kiswahili. Funding splits evenly: $80 million from the Kenyan government, $80 million from dozens of private donors, including billionaire heirs to the Walton and Cargill family fortunes. The money flows through a Project Finance for Permanence (PFP) model, which ties disbursements to verifiable government policy changes rather than goodwill commitments.

Four focus zones

The initiative will start in four geographic areas. Tsavo, Kenya’s largest national park complex, holds 40 percent of the country’s elephants and 20 percent of its critically endangered black rhinos. A southern zone along the Tanzanian border spans the Maasai Mara and links into the Serengeti, a corridor that wildlife has used for seasonal migration long before either country drew its borders. The Great Rift Valley and two additional hotspots round out the four.

What PFP requires

Conservation funding has a recurring problem: it arrives, gets spent, and produces little that changes policy or land status. The PFP model is a structural attempt to fix that. Money is conditional on the government hitting specific policy benchmarks, not delivered up front. Brazil and Gabon signed similar agreements last year. Namibia and Botswana are in the works. Kenya’s deal is among the largest yet.

Closing the 30×30 gap

Kenya has committed to the global “30×30” target: 30 percent of land and sea protected by 2030. The Nature Conservancy puts current coverage at 20 to 23 percent. Ryan Bidwell, who runs TNC’s PFP program, said this deal would largely close the distance.

The economic case is also there. A UN Environment Programme report drew on Kenyan government data showing that roughly 42 percent of the country’s GDP and 70 percent of its employment depend on nature in some form. Cabinet Secretary for Tourism and Wildlife Rebecca Miano said the program would benefit both wildlife and the farming communities that work these landscapes.

“There is a substantial gap that would be largely closed,” Bidwell said. Whether it closes depends on Kenya delivering on the policy commitments the funding is tied to, something that’s far harder to sidestep under PFP than under a conventional grant.

articles.title: Higher Ground: How New York is raising a park to hold back the sea
articles.summary: On 29 October 2012, Hurricane Sandy slammed into New York City, unleashing a devastating storm surge that flooded homes, subways and tunnels, knocked out power and sparked deadly fires.
articles.content:
In just 48 hours, 44 people were killed, nearly two million New Yorkers lost power, and 6,500 patients were evacuated from hospitals and nursing homes.

New York swore: never again.

But as climate change threatened to bring in ever more extreme weather, and to dangerously raise sea levels around the coastal city, “never again” meant building ambitious resiliency infrastructure all along the city’s coastline.

Fourteen years after Sandy, UN News visited one section of the multibillion-dollar project: the East Side Coastal Resiliency (ESCR) Project.

© NYCDDC

What lies beneath

North of the Williamsburg Bridge, a white crane hoists buckets of fill off a barge and tips them into waiting earth movers. Load by load, the East River Park is being raised as much as 10 feet (three metres).

The park is one link in a chain of flood defences rising along more than three miles (five kilometres) of Manhattan’s waterfront. Conceived after Hurricane Sandy swamped the area in 2012, the East Side Coastal Resiliency project and a smaller companion to the south – a roughly $2 billion investment – are designed to protect more than 110,000 residents.

“This whole place was inundated,” said Bobby Issac, Assistant Commissioner of Coastal Resiliency Construction at the city’s Department of Design and Construction.

During Sandy, he recalled, at least a storey of the public housing blocks behind him was underwater, and residents could not get in or out.

Here, most of the protection is out of sight. A floodwall runs hidden through the heart of the rebuilt park. At the water’s edge, concrete-filled piles plunge about 100ft (30m) into reclaimed land that can hide anything from old piers to the remains of ships.

“What you see on the top is only a third of what is built,” Mr. Issac said.

When a storm approaches, nothing in the park needs to move. Elsewhere along the waterfront, crews will swing or slide 18 floodgates shut, and farther south nearly 100 flip-up barriers will be raised. The design also builds in about 30 inches (76 centimetres) for rising seas, he said.

With about 90 per cent of the system in place, temporary barriers can plug any gaps at a few days’ notice until work ends in 2027, he added.

Beyond Sandy

UN News/Daniel Dickinson

In addition to the lives lost, Sandy caused $19 billion in damage, recalled Kathryn Prybylski, New York City’s Assistant Commissioner of the Bureau of Coastal Resilience, who will operate the new walls and gates.

“These projects that are in construction now around the city are kind of a reaction to Sandy,” she said. “It’s really time for us now to look to the future.”

The wider picture adds urgency. According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the rate of global sea level rise has nearly doubled since satellite measurements began in 1993, while warming oceans are fuelling more intense tropical storms.

For a city with 520mi (840km) of coastline, the threat is not only the next superstorm but also the everyday tide. Without protective measures, Ms. Prybylski warned, many New Yorkers will face regular tidal flooding in the decades ahead.

Soundcloud

“By regular, that could mean in some locations once a month, twice a month, 10 times a month,” she said. Eventually, she added, some streets could flood with the tide every day – changing how people get to work and how they send their children to school.

The tip of the iceberg

New York is only one of the cities facing these threats.

© Adobe Stock/Solepsizm

Nearly 10 per cent of the world’s population – some 770 million people – live in coastal areas less than five metres (16.4ft) above the high tide and are thus heavily exposed, a recent UN report found.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres has warned that “mega-cities on every continent will face serious impacts” from rising seas, naming New York among them.

“[New York’s flood defence project] is a commendable step forward. It's also a message to all big cities,” Navid Hanif, from the UN’s Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA), told UN News.

“What New York is doing should be acknowledged, appreciated and emulated in other parts of the world,” he said.

Importantly, while rising seas primarily threaten infrastructure in high-income cities like New York, Miami and China’s Guangzhou, they pose an existential threat to communities in low-lying South Asian cities such as Kolkata, Mumbai and Dhaka.

Over 14 million people in South Asia risk losing their homes to permanent inundation, while communities in Fiji, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands and other low-lying Pacific islands have already been forced to relocate.

Adaptation, adaptation, adaptation

The UN, whose headquarters are only less than two miles north of the ESCR, is an active partner, supporting mitigation and adaptation efforts worldwide.

At a recent meeting on sea level rise, Member States adopted the UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise, the first time all Member States have agreed on a single, common text on the issue.

The Declaration notably called for more predictable and accessible funding for adaptation and resilience, especially for small islands and least developed countries.

New York’s East Side Coastal Resiliency project offers a glimpse of what such investments can mean for local communities.

© NYCDDC

In the now-elevated East River Park, strollers enjoy riverside walking paths looking onto the Brooklyn skyline, along with neatly trimmed green areas and community spaces including sports fields, playgrounds and barbecuing spots.

“We're in this park twice a day, every day. We love it! It's a beautiful example of how climate resilience can help people enjoy their lives,” said Liz, a passer-by from the neighbourhood walking her dog.

The story is focused, detailed, and clearly illustrates a positive real-world impact on public safety and urban resilience.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that magma deep inside Earth can store surprising amounts of extra oxygen, potentially revealing a hidden contributor to our planet's oxygen-rich atmosphere. The findings suggest that ancient volcanic eruptions may have helped transform Earth's atmosphere billions of years ago, with implications for understanding life on other planets.
articles.content:
Scientists have discovered that molten rock deep inside Earth can store far more oxygen than previously believed. The finding challenges long-standing assumptions about magma and raises an intriguing possibility: oxygen released from Earth's interior may have helped transform the planet's atmosphere billions of years ago.

Through high-pressure experiments and advanced computer simulations, researchers found that magma can absorb additional oxygen beyond the amount normally required by its chemical composition. This hidden oxygen could provide a previously unrecognized connection between Earth's deep interior, volcanic activity, and the development of an oxygen-rich atmosphere.

The research was led by Dr. Yanhao Lin and Dr. Ho-kwang Mao of the Center for High Pressure Science and Technology Advanced Research (HPSTAR), working with Prof. Haiyang Niu of Northwestern Polytechnical University and Prof. Wim van Westrenen of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Their findings were published in National Science Review.

Scientists Challenge a Long-Standing Assumption About Magma

Oxygen is one of the most abundant elements inside Earth, accounting for more than half of the atoms in the planet's silicate interior. Silicates are minerals and molten materials composed primarily of silicon and oxygen, along with other elements. They make up much of Earth's mantle and crust.

Despite oxygen's abundance, scientists have traditionally assumed that magma can contain only a specific amount of it. Under this understanding, the oxygen content is determined by the quantities and electrical charge states of other elements in the molten rock, including silicon, magnesium, and iron.

Water and carbon dioxide behave differently. Both can dissolve in magma and later escape as gases when the surrounding pressure decreases. These substances are known as volatile components, and their release plays an important role in volcanic activity.

Oxygen, however, has generally not been treated as a separate volatile substance that magma can absorb and release. Whether molten silicate rock could hold additional oxygen independently of its ordinary chemical composition remained largely unexplored.

The new research suggests that this assumption may need to change.

Extreme Pressure Reveals Hidden Oxygen in Molten Rock

To investigate, the scientists recreated conditions found deep within Earth using laboratory equipment capable of generating extraordinary pressures and temperatures.

They heated a synthetic version of mid-ocean ridge basalt, a type of volcanic rock commonly produced where tectonic plates move apart beneath the oceans. The samples were exposed to pressures ranging from normal atmospheric pressure to 7 gigapascals and temperatures between 1200 and 1800 °C.

A pressure of 7 gigapascals is approximately 69,000 times the atmospheric pressure at Earth's surface.

The team used specialized piston-cylinder and cubic presses to maintain these extreme conditions. They also added platinum oxide (PtO2) to establish an oxygen-rich environment and test how much additional oxygen the molten rock could absorb.

After the experiments, the researchers rapidly cooled the molten material, producing glass that preserved important characteristics of the melt. They then analyzed its elemental composition and measured the amounts of water and carbon dioxide present.

By calculating how much oxygen was needed to balance the other elements, along with the oxygen already contained in water and carbon dioxide, the scientists could estimate how much remained unaccounted for.

They called this additional amount "excess oxygen."

The results revealed a striking relationship between pressure and oxygen storage.

At normal atmospheric pressure, the glass contained almost no excess oxygen. At 7 gigapascals, however, excess oxygen accounted for more than 5% of the sample's weight.

For comparison, experiments conducted at similar pressures and temperatures without added platinum oxide produced excess oxygen concentrations of only 0.2% to 0.5% by weight.

The researchers also wanted to determine whether the additional oxygen was truly incorporated into the material or merely trapped as tiny gas bubbles.

Using Raman spectroscopy, a technique that identifies substances by examining how they interact with light, they found no detectable signature of oxygen gas in the glass. This indicated that the excess oxygen had become part of the glass structure rather than accumulating in bubbles.

The measured concentrations may even underestimate magma's actual oxygen-storage capacity. Some oxygen could have escaped while the molten samples were cooling, meaning the original melts may have contained still greater amounts.

Computer Simulations Reveal How Magma Stores Extra Oxygen

To better understand the discovery at the atomic level, Prof. Niu led a series of theoretical computer simulations.

The researchers used deep neural network (DNN) models to simulate interactions among atoms with accuracy approaching that of ab initio calculations, which describe atomic behavior using fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

The simulations showed that additional oxygen could dissolve into molten material until the system reached equilibrium, a state in which oxygen entering and leaving the melt is balanced.

Although the computer models used a simplified system containing only magnesium, silicon, and oxygen, they reproduced the same overall pattern observed in the laboratory: magma's ability to hold excess oxygen increased with pressure.

The simulated oxygen concentrations were lower than the experimental measurements, which the scientists attributed to differences between the simplified model and the more complex chemical composition of actual basalt.

The calculations also revealed changes in how oxygen atoms behaved as more oxygen entered the melt. Their electrical charges became more varied, and a small proportion formed peroxide-like bonds, in which oxygen atoms bond to one another.

These changes help explain how molten rock might accommodate oxygen beyond the amount predicted by conventional chemical models.

Importantly, the pressure-dependent behavior resembles that of water and carbon dioxide, which also become more soluble in magma as pressure increases.

Based on these findings, the researchers propose that oxygen should be recognized as an independent component of silicate melts, rather than being considered only in relation to other elements.

Could Ancient Volcanoes Have Helped Oxygenate Earth's Atmosphere?

The discovery raises a much larger question about Earth's history: Could magma have transported significant amounts of oxygen from the planet's interior to its surface?

The researchers suggest a possible mechanism involving magma generated in oxidized regions of Earth's mantle.

Under the immense pressures deep underground, this magma could absorb substantial quantities of excess oxygen. As it moves upward, the surrounding pressure decreases, reducing the amount of oxygen the molten rock can retain.

Some of that oxygen could then be released, potentially contributing to chemical reactions that increase the oxidation of the upper mantle, Earth's crust, and eventually the atmosphere.

Oxidation refers to chemical processes involving the transfer of electrons. In this context, oxygen carried by magma could increase the oxidizing capacity of surrounding materials and potentially influence the balance of oxygen in the atmosphere.

This proposed mechanism may also help explain an intriguing coincidence in Earth's geological past.

Between approximately 2.5 billion and 2.0 billion years ago, atmospheric oxygen levels underwent major increases. This interval overlaps with the formation of some of Earth's largest large igneous provinces (LIPs), enormous regions of volcanic rock created by exceptionally large outpourings of magma.

The researchers suggest that oxygen released from these ancient volcanic systems could have contributed to changes in atmospheric composition.

Their preliminary calculation highlights the potentially enormous scale of the process. They estimate that if magma erupted during this period released excess oxygen equal to just 0.27% of its weight, the total amount could theoretically match all the oxygen present in Earth's atmosphere today.

This does not establish that volcanic activity actually supplied that much atmospheric oxygen. Instead, it illustrates how even a relatively small release of oxygen from immense quantities of magma could have major planetary consequences.

A New Clue to Earth's Evolution and Habitable Planets

The findings could influence several important areas of planetary science.

For one, they may change how scientists understand ancient magma oceans, vast regions of molten rock believed to have existed during the early evolution of Earth and other rocky planets.

They also introduce a possible new factor in volcanic degassing, the process through which gases and other volatile substances escape from molten rock and interact with a planet's atmosphere.

If magma can store and release oxygen independently of its other chemical components, models of Earth's atmospheric development may need to account for this previously overlooked process.

The implications could extend beyond Earth. Understanding how oxygen moves between the interiors and atmospheres of rocky planets may help researchers investigate the conditions that allow potentially habitable environments to develop and persist over billions of years.

Although further research is needed to establish how much oxygen natural magmas carry and how much reaches the atmosphere, the discovery points to a surprising possibility: some of the processes that helped shape Earth's oxygen-rich environment may have originated far beneath the planet's surface.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery revealing that magma deep inside Earth can store and release excess oxygen, which may have contributed to the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere billions of years ago. This finding challenges previous assumptions, has broad implications for understanding Earth's atmospheric evolution and planetary habitability, and represents a meaningful breakthrough in geoscience with potential large-scale impact on environmental and planetary science.
articles.personality_title: Scientists find hidden oxygen in Earth’s molten rock, changing how we understand our atmosphere
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long believed that magma, the molten rock inside Earth, contains a fixed amount of oxygen based on its chemical makeup. Oxygen is a major part of Earth's interior, but unlike water or carbon dioxide, it was not thought to be stored or released independently by magma.

**What happened** – A team of researchers recreated the high pressures and temperatures found deep inside Earth using special lab equipment. They heated volcanic rock samples with extra oxygen and found that magma can actually hold much more oxygen than expected—over 5% by weight at very high pressure. They confirmed this oxygen was part of the molten rock itself, not just trapped gas bubbles. Computer simulations supported these results and showed how oxygen atoms behave differently when extra oxygen is present.

**Impact** – This discovery suggests that magma deep underground can carry and release oxygen, possibly affecting Earth's atmosphere. Ancient volcanic eruptions might have released oxygen from inside Earth, helping increase the oxygen in the air billions of years ago. This challenges old ideas about how oxygen moved to the surface and could change how scientists study Earth’s history and the atmospheres of other planets.

**What's next step** – Researchers will study how much oxygen magma normally carries and how much reaches the surface during eruptions. They will also explore how this process influenced Earth's atmosphere over time and whether it affects other rocky planets, improving our understanding of planetary habitability.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists discovered that magma deep inside Earth can store extra oxygen, which may have helped shape our oxygen-rich atmosphere long ago.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques découvrent de l’oxygène caché dans la roche en fusion au cœur de la Terre
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – On pensait longtemps que le magma, la roche en fusion à l’intérieur de la Terre, contenait une quantité d’oxygène fixe basée sur sa composition chimique. L’oxygène est un élément majeur à l’intérieur de la Terre, mais on ne croyait pas qu’il puisse être stocké ou libéré indépendamment par le magma, contrairement à l’eau ou au dioxyde de carbone.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe de chercheurs a recréé en laboratoire les hautes pressions et températures présentes profondément dans la Terre. Ils ont chauffé des échantillons de roche volcanique avec de l’oxygène supplémentaire et ont découvert que le magma peut contenir beaucoup plus d’oxygène que prévu—plus de 5 % en poids sous très haute pression. Ils ont confirmé que cet oxygène faisait bien partie du magma, et n’était pas simplement emprisonné sous forme de bulles de gaz. Des simulations informatiques ont confirmé ces résultats et montré comment les atomes d’oxygène se comportent différemment avec cet excès.

**Impact** – Cette découverte suggère que le magma profond peut transporter et libérer de l’oxygène, ce qui pourrait avoir influencé l’atmosphère terrestre. Les anciennes éruptions volcaniques auraient pu libérer de l’oxygène provenant de l’intérieur de la Terre, contribuant à l’augmentation de l’oxygène dans l’air il y a des milliards d’années. Cela remet en question les idées anciennes sur le transfert de l’oxygène à la surface et pourrait changer la manière dont les scientifiques étudient l’histoire de la Terre et les atmosphères d’autres planètes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont étudier la quantité d’oxygène que le magma transporte normalement et combien atteint la surface lors des éruptions. Ils examineront aussi l’impact de ce processus sur l’atmosphère terrestre à travers le temps et sur d’autres planètes rocheuses, afin de mieux comprendre les conditions favorables à la vie.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont découvert que le magma profond peut stocker de l’oxygène supplémentaire, ce qui aurait pu contribuer à former notre atmosphère riche en oxygène il y a longtemps.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren oxígeno oculto en la roca fundida dentro de la Tierra
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, se pensó que el magma, la roca fundida dentro de la Tierra, contenía una cantidad fija de oxígeno basada en su composición química. El oxígeno es un elemento abundante en el interior de la Tierra, pero no se creía que el magma pudiera almacenar o liberar oxígeno por sí mismo, a diferencia del agua o el dióxido de carbono.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo de investigadores recreó en laboratorio las altas presiones y temperaturas que existen en las profundidades de la Tierra. Calentaron muestras de roca volcánica con oxígeno extra y descubrieron que el magma puede contener mucho más oxígeno del esperado—más del 5 % en peso a presiones muy altas. Confirmaron que este oxígeno estaba incorporado en la roca fundida y no atrapado en burbujas de gas. Simulaciones por computadora apoyaron estos resultados y mostraron cómo los átomos de oxígeno cambian su comportamiento con el oxígeno adicional.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo sugiere que el magma profundo puede transportar y liberar oxígeno, lo que podría haber afectado la atmósfera de la Tierra. Las antiguas erupciones volcánicas podrían haber liberado oxígeno desde el interior de la Tierra, ayudando a aumentar el oxígeno en el aire hace miles de millones de años. Esto desafía ideas antiguas sobre cómo el oxígeno llegó a la superficie y podría cambiar cómo los científicos estudian la historia de la Tierra y las atmósferas de otros planetas.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores estudiarán cuánto oxígeno suele contener el magma y cuánto llega a la superficie durante las erupciones. También explorarán cómo este proceso influyó en la atmósfera terrestre con el tiempo y en otros planetas rocosos, para mejorar la comprensión sobre la habitabilidad planetaria.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos descubrieron que el magma profundo puede almacenar oxígeno extra, lo que pudo haber ayudado a formar nuestra atmósfera rica en oxígeno hace mucho tiempo.

articles.title: Blue Planet III is the best yet from the BBC and David Attenborough
articles.summary: The BBC has another game-changing hit in Blue Planet III, says Michael Le Page, with David Attenborough narrating and a smart dolphin
articles.content:
A southern right whale in Blue Planet III BBC Studios

Blue Planet III

BBC One/BBC iPlayer From 1 November

The trouble with making two incredible, groundbreaking television series about life in the oceans is that it sets a very high bar. Blue Planet III was always going to be good, but how good? I’m delighted to report that the BBC’s Natural History Unit has outdone itself. The latest series is better in just about every way, and yet another must-watch.

The focus for the third series was finding new behaviours to film. “I’m very pleased to say that, in Blue Planet III, you really have not seen it before,” said series commissioner Jack Bootle at an early screening that also featured a Q&A with the production team. “This series is bursting with novel behaviours, and even a few strange new animals.”

Advertisement

Based on the first three episodes, that last statement rings true. Perhaps the most striking example is a 40-year-old, pregnant dolphin filmed in Shark Bay in Australia. “We called her Gambara after [an] Aboriginal word for clever,” said Yoland Bosiger, who produced the first episode.

The team focused on Gambara because she is often seen with a sponge cupped over her beak. This sponge-carrying behaviour was first seen in dolphins in the area in 1984. It is known to be passed from mother to daughter, but why? The idea has been that the sponges protect the beaks of the dolphins as they hunt for fish beneath the sand. This may be true of some dolphins, but what Gambara does is far more impressive.

On Shark Bay’s sandy bottom are small outcrops of coral a metre or so across in which fish hide when Gambara chases them. She notes the hole where they enter. Then, when the fish have left their hiding place, she blocks the entrance with the sponge. The next time she chases the fish, they dash for the hole only to swim into an unexpected obstacle, making it easy for Gambara to snap them up.

In other words, this hunting strategy involves understanding how prey will behave and using a tool to set a trap. Clever indeed.

Gambara the dolphin blocks the entrance of the hiding place with a sponge, making the fish easy to snap up

“There have been inferences about what the hunting behaviour is, but nobody’s been able to see it with their own eyes,” said Bosiger. Filming it wasn’t easy: being in the right place at the right time would be hard, so the team set up fixed cameras around some of the coral outcrops. But off-the-shelf cameras kept flooding and didn’t record for long enough. Instead, the BBC developed cameras especially for the task.

Indeed, the camerawork really stands out, thanks in part to technical advances like this. “There has been a huge amount of development over the last 10 years since Blue Planet II,” said series producer Lara Bickerton.

One scene features a Maori wrasse, with gorgeous close-ups revealing the dazzling patterns on the fish’s skin. When the wrasse breaks through corals in search of smaller fish, the scene is also filmed from inside the corals looking up. At one point, the camera even seems to enter the wrasse’s mouth.

A Harlequin shrimp in Blue Planet III BBC Studios

Another extraordinary scene shows a sick female humpback whale, plagued by dozens of fish called remoras that are attached to her. Then the drone shot widens out: the whale is surrounded by hundreds of sharks, biding their time. In the oceans, you don’t get to die in peace.

Advances in technology also allowed the series to be made in a different way, said executive producer Elizabeth White. Where possible, producers worked remotely with local teams, cutting back on the need for flights. “An awful lot goes into thinking about being sustainable,” she said.

David Attenborough narrates this series again – it wouldn’t be the same without him. “He’s still very much involved in working with our script. He basically changed every single line,” said Bosiger. “He adds so much personality and humour.” But to me, he is starting to sound his age, so there’s a tinge of sadness on hearing his changed voice.

The first series of The Blue Planet was shown in 2001, followed by Blue Planet II in 2017 – remember the pilot whale carrying her dead calf? The series were so influential in stimulating interest in ocean life and concern about marine pollution (especially plastic) that people began to talk of “the Blue Planet effect”. From what I have seen, this series will have a similar impact. It’s a stunning triumph. Well done, BBC.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the release of Blue Planet III, a groundbreaking nature documentary series that showcases novel ocean behaviors and advances in filming technology, raising public awareness about marine life and environmental issues. It has broad significance for society by inspiring conservation and understanding of ocean ecosystems.
articles.personality_title: Blue Planet III reveals new ocean secrets with stunning footage and smart dolphins
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The BBC has created two famous nature series about ocean life, Blue Planet and Blue Planet II, which showed amazing underwater scenes and helped people learn about the sea.

**What happened** – On November 1, Blue Planet III was released, featuring even more new and unusual behaviors of ocean animals. One example is a clever dolphin named Gambara who uses a sponge as a tool to trap fish by blocking their hiding spots. The filmmakers used specially made cameras to capture scenes that no one had seen before, like close-up views inside coral and a whale surrounded by sharks.

**Impact** – This series is special because it shows never-before-seen animal actions and uses new technology to film the ocean in ways that feel fresh and exciting. It also continues the work of raising awareness about ocean life and environmental challenges, encouraging people to care more about protecting the seas.

**What's next step** – The series will be available on BBC One and BBC iPlayer, where many people can watch and learn from it. Its success may inspire more films that use advanced technology to explore nature and help protect marine environments.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Blue Planet III offers groundbreaking views of ocean life with smart animal behaviors and new filming technology, continuing to inspire understanding and care for the sea.
articles.personality_title_fr: Blue Planet III dévoile de nouveaux secrets marins avec des images époustouflantes et des dauphins intelligents
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La BBC a créé deux célèbres séries sur la vie océanique, Blue Planet et Blue Planet II, qui montraient des scènes sous-marines incroyables et ont aidé le public à mieux connaître la mer.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 1er novembre, Blue Planet III est sorti, présentant encore plus de comportements nouveaux et inhabituels d’animaux marins. Un exemple est un dauphin intelligent nommé Gambara qui utilise une éponge comme outil pour piéger les poissons en bloquant leurs cachettes. Les réalisateurs ont utilisé des caméras spécialement conçues pour filmer des scènes jamais vues auparavant, comme des gros plans à l’intérieur des coraux et une baleine entourée de requins.

**Impact** – Cette série est spéciale car elle montre des actions animales inédites et utilise une nouvelle technologie pour filmer l’océan de manière fraîche et captivante. Elle continue aussi à sensibiliser le public à la vie marine et aux défis environnementaux, encourageant à protéger les océans.

**Prochaine étape** – La série sera disponible sur BBC One et BBC iPlayer, où beaucoup pourront la regarder et apprendre. Son succès pourrait inspirer d’autres films utilisant la technologie avancée pour explorer la nature et protéger les milieux marins.

**Message en une phrase** – Blue Planet III offre des vues révolutionnaires de la vie océanique avec des comportements d’animaux intelligents et une nouvelle technologie de tournage, poursuivant l’inspiration pour comprendre et protéger la mer.
articles.personality_title_es: Blue Planet III revela nuevos secretos del océano con impresionantes imágenes y delfines inteligentes

**Resumen en una frase** – Blue Planet III ofrece vistas innovadoras de la vida oceánica con comportamientos inteligentes y nueva tecnología de filmación, continuando la inspiración para entender y cuidar el mar.
